paper_title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

sections.content: Can vision-language model look at picture of chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 8292% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, fluent account of scene is thus no evidence of correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do. The benchmark, its generator and the evaluation code are available at https://huggingface. co/datasets/emilioferrara/DominoBench. 1 1. Introduction Vision-language models have become common interface between machines and pictures of the physical world: they answer questions about photographs and diagrams, and they are increasingly asked to act in physical environments, where describing scene well does not translate into predicting it [8, 52]. Acting rests on an ability that is rarely tested directly, namely predicting what scene will do next. model that sees ball at the top of ramp, ledge, pendulum and row of dominoes should be able to say where the ball goes, what it hits, and who is in its way. Physical reasoning benchmarks have probed this ability for years, through interactive puzzles, videos and textbook questions [2, 5, 8, 37, 54, 56], and recent benchmarks have begun to ask for forward prediction from single image [28, 43, 46]. Figure 1 shows the kind of scene that exposes the limits of current models. pushed ball sets off two rows of dominoes, and small ball at the end of the chain drops into the bucket of seesaw whose spikes hang over person, C, lying on the ground. The two items of the pair differ in one quantity, the width of the stone counterweight on the other arm of the seesaw. In item (a) it is 1.25 grid squares, the ball in the bucket outweighs it, and the spikes come down on C. In item (b) it is 1.50 squares and the seesaw does not tip. Unaided, Claude Opus 5.5 describes plausible chain reaction and gets both items wrong, predicting that dies in (b) and survives in (a). Given the calculation that decides the outcome, it gets both right. The scene is easy to see and the calculation is short. What the model lacks is the step from the picture to the number that decides the outcome. Existing benchmarks rarely isolate this failure: their items depend on one mechanism, unfold over video, or do not sit close enough to tipping point for the qualitative chain reaction to be wrong. This paper asks whether multimodal models can predict the outcome of multi-step chain reaction from single still image, and where they fail when they cannot. To answer it we built DominoBench, generator and benchmark of 2D rigid-body scenes in which single push starts chain of three to five mechanisms drawn from seven: ledges with drop, pits, pendulums, notched balls rolling past persons head, seesaws with spikes, rows of dominoes and jumps, joined by ramps  (Fig. 1)  . Every scene is built and settled by physics simulator, which also produces the ground truth. Every item has minimal-pair twin in which one quantity, such as the height of ledge or the width of pit, differs by one to three grid steps and the fate of one person flips. Every item is posed along four-rung hint ladder, from no hint, to generic nudge, to pointer at the deciding step, to the exact calculation that decides the outcome, and in text-only mode that replaces the picture with its exact geometry. The ladder and the text-only mode probe three abilities that single accuracy figure conflates: noticing which quanWe tity matters, reading it from the scene, and carrying out the calculation once its inputs are given. To rank models on one scale we define DominoScore, weighted geometric mean of chance-corrected accuracy over the mechanisms, in which harder mechanisms weigh more. evaluated 30 models from 10 families on DominoBench-1K, the full benchmark of 854 items in 427 minimal pairs over 7 deciding mechanisms, and on the medium DominoBench-124; we also release DominoBench-38, small, quick-to-run test set (supplementary material). Our experiments lead to four findings. (i) Unaided, no model predicts these scenes reliably: the four Claude models that answered all 854 items are right about the full outcome in at most 47% of items, about the person whose fate flips in 5761%, and about both twins of pair in at most 16%. (ii) The failure is quantitative. Pointing model at the deciding step helps little, while writing out the calculation and its inputs, some of which still image cannot show, raises accuracy on the deciding person to 8286%. (iii) Misreading the picture explains little of the unaided errors: on DominoBench-124, with the exact geometry given as text, the Claude 5.5 models gain at most 6 points unaided. (iv) The pattern holds across providers on DominoBench-124, although the GPT models gain least from the calculation, and the full calculation separates models that can execute it, including most larger open-weight models, from small open-weight models that stay near chance in image mode even when it is written out. DominoBench-1K, with its images, structured scene descriptions, simulator trajectories, hint ladders and twins, is publicly available together with the generator and the evaluation harness at https://huggingface.co/ datasets/emilioferrara/DominoBench. 2. Related work Physical reasoning benchmarks. Benchmarks for physical reasoning began with agents and videos [29]: placing objects in 2D simulated scene until goal is reached [2], detecting violations of object permanence [7, 37], and answering predictive, causal and counterfactual questions about collisions, rolling and dominoes in video [1, 3, 5, 44, 54]; video generators still produce physically wrong outcomes [31]. Predicting dynamics from single still has shorter history, from Newtonian scenarios for one object [32] to the stability of block stacks [4, 15]. With visionlanguage models, the field turned to question answering: PhysBench and PhysVista probe properties, relations and dynamics [8, 33], QuantiPhy asks for physical quantities [34], PhysReason, SeePhys and PHYBench pose multi-step exam problems [35, 51, 56], causal benchmarks probe interventions on static scenes [11, 19], and multimodal models fall short of humans on block-tower stability, causal judgments and the conservation of quantities [27, 39]. The closest recent work predicts outcomes from one image: billiard trajectories with secondary collisions from the initial frame [46], what puzzle-game contraption does once started, from screenshot [43], and the center of mass, lever equilibrium and Newtons first law [28]. We know of no earlier benchmark combining simulated multi-mechanism causal chains in single still image with tipping-point minimal pairs, hint ladder and an exact text rendering. Perception and modality in vision-language models. Vision-language models often fail to read exact geometry from an image, such as whether two lines cross or two circles touch [10, 36, 42], quantitative visual reasoning in mathematics remains hard [26], and models that recognize the content of an image often cannot infer what transformation of it would show [48]. Studies that present the same content as an image and as text find that models frequently do better from text [9, 47, 55]. Like these studies, we give every item an exact text rendering, to test whether misreading the picture explains prediction errors. Minimal pairs. Contrast sets and counterfactual edits probe models decision boundary with small changes that flip the label [12, 18], and paired items with opposite answers expose models that rely on priors in visual question answering [13, 22, 41]. In physical understanding, Minimal Video Pairs scores models on curated video twins with opposite answers [20], vision-language models keep the same choice when the deciding measurement in an image pair changes [38], and GeoFlip pairs scenes in which one geometric change flips simulated one-step event for video generators [24]. We know of no benchmark that builds such twins for causal chains in still images, by stepping one visible parameter across simulated tipping point. Hints and the evaluation of reasoning. Step-by-step and progressive-hint prompting improve multi-step problem solving [49, 57], process-level evaluation judges intermediate steps as well as final answers [25, 40, 45], PhysicsMind conditions answers on the relevant physical law [28], GRIP locates failures with ladder of compositional subquestions [16], and in text-only physics, errors arise more often in building the model of problem than in solving it [53]. The DominoBench hint ladder instead adds graded external information, from generic nudge to pointer at the deciding step to the deciding calculation itself, so that the rung at which model starts to succeed indicates what it is missing. Procedural generation with simulator follows CLEVR and Kubric [14, 17], and allows regeneration from fresh seeds, defense against contamination [30, 50]. 3. DominoBench DominoBench items are built from physics: simulator composes scene, lets it settle, and renders the settled state, so the picture always shows scene at rest and the ground truth is what the physics does once the ball is pushed. Scenes. scene is side view of terrain on visible grid, with one unit per grid square, populated by people labelled to F. Person stands at the top and pushes ball, stone or wood, full or with crescent notch cut out of it. The ball then passes through chain of three to five mechanisms drawn from library of seven, each of which can kill one person: ledge, where the ball flies off drop and may clear or hit person standing below; pit, where person crouches inside gap the ball may or may not jump; pendulum, hanging ball that the arriving ball sets swinging toward person; recess, where persons head sticks out of cage and survives only if the balls notch faces down as it passes; seesaw with downward spikes, which the ball may or may not tip onto person lying underneath; row of dominoes, which may or may not fall far enough to reach person or hand off to second ball; and jump, kicker that launches the ball over wall. Each mechanism is parameterized part with continuous placement parameters such as the height of drop, the width of pit, the length of pendulum, the gap between dominoes, or the counterweight on seesaw. scene program, stored as plain JSON, lists the parts and their parameters and builds deterministically in pymunk [6]. The rules of the world are stated with every item: 2D rigid bodies with mass equal to density times area (stone 2.5, wood 0.6 per unit area), balls rolling without slipping except when skidding after landing, gravity of 9.81 squares/s2, push that sets the first ball rolling at 1.5 squares/s, and person who dies when any moving solid object touches them and who neither moves nor stops objects. The last rule is convention that keeps every outcome categorical and readable from the trajectory. Generation checks. Every item passes five checks before it enters the benchmark. The settle check runs the scene without the push and rejects it if anything moves more than 0.05 squares or touches person, and the trigger and chain checks confirm that the push starts the chain and reaches at least three mechanisms in both twins. The stability check repeats the simulation at half the timestep with twice the solver iterations, with friction scaled by 0.9 and 1.1, and with elasticity raised by 0.05, and rejects the item if any persons fate changes. The solvability check, described below, guarantees that an idealized calculation on the quantities stated in the H3 hint reproduces both outcomes. 3 Minimal pairs at tipping point. Each item has twin that differs in one placement parameter of one mechanism, by one to three grid steps (lengths step by 0.25 squares), and in which only the person whom that mechanism can kill changes fate while every other persons fate stays the same. Twins are found by guided search. From one simulation of the base scene we read the quantities that each mechanisms outcome depends on, such as the speed of the ball as it arrives at ledge or the number of rotations it has completed when it reaches recess. With those quantities fixed, an idealized calculation for each mechanism gives the persons fate as function of the mechanisms own placement parameter: projectile against box for the ledge, projectile against the far rim for the pit, energy and reach for the pendulum, gap against domino height for the dominoes, rotation phase against simulation-calibrated notch window for the recess, torque about the pivot for the seesaw, and launch trajectory against the wall for the jump. The search places twins on either side of the predicted threshold and keeps pair only if simulation confirms the flip, agrees with the idealized calculation on both twins, leaves every other fate unchanged, and passes the stability check on both. This is the solvability check: for every kept pair, short calculation on quantities that can be read from the grid or are stated in the H3 hint, including arrival speeds measured in the simulation, predicts both outcomes, so the H3 hint never points to wrong answer. Visible deaths. persons collision box reaches slightly beyond the drawn figure near its corners, so we removed every pair in which labelled death comes from body that enters the box without touching the figure (73 of 500 generated pairs, mostly at ledges, and 6 of 25 in the small benchmark; supplementary material). DominoBench1K keeps 427 pairs; the medium and small benchmarks, named by their remaining items, are DominoBench-124 and DominoBench-38. The DominoScore weights (Section 4) are computed after this filter. Of the 427 pairs, 89 differ by one grid step, 208 by two and 130 by three. Items. Each item consists of the rendered still, structured scene description that gives every objects shape, material and position in grid units, the question Who dies if pushes the ball?, the simulated answer for every person, the full simulator trajectory and contact log, the deciding mechanism and parameter, the identifier of its twin, the hint ladder, and the list of assumptions. Answers are categorical per person; an item is correct only if every fate is right. The hint ladder. Every item is posed at four rungs, each in fresh context. At H0 the model receives the image, the rules and the question, and the instructions already ask it to work through the chain and to check any quantity that could change the outcome. H1 adds generic nudge (Before answering, consider the quantitative details in the picture that could change the outcome). H2 points at the deciding step without saying what happens there (for pair 4: Consider whether the ball landing in the bucket can outweigh the counterweight above C). H3 states the idealized calculation for that step with the quantities it needs, including those that cannot be read from still image, such as the turning effect with which the empty seesaw holds its arm up (. . . The empty seesaw (plank, bucket, spikes and stone counterweight together) holds its left arm up with turning effect of about 1.85. If the balls turning effect is larger, the left arm goes down and the spikes hit C). H3 never states the answer. The model still has to carry out the calculation, compare the result with the persons position, and propagate it through the rest of the chain. By construction of the solvability check, the H3 calculation predicts the simulated fate of the deciding person on all 854 items. We compare H0 with H2 for the benefit of locating the deciding step, and H2 with H3 for the benefit of the calculation. Text-only mode. Each item can also be posed without the image, with the structured scene description serialized as text, including exact coordinates. Text mode removes the need to read positions from pixels, so comparing the two modes tests whether misreading the picture explains errors. DominoBench-1K. The full benchmark, DominoBench1K, contains 427 pairs (854 items), with 62 to 70 pairs for each of the 7 deciding mechanisms except the ledge, which keeps 27 (Section 3, visible deaths). Chains have three mechanisms in 489 items, four in 238 and five in 127, and items show 2 to 6 people and kill between 0 and 3 of them. The naive chain-reaction answer, in which everyone except the pusher dies, is wrong for 731 of the 854 items. The generator, the scene programs and the random seeds are released with the benchmark, so new items can be drawn from held-out seeds whenever contamination becomes concern. Building DominoBench-1K took about 10.7 hours of wallclock time on single machine running 14 search processes in parallel (at most about 150 CPU-hours). 4. Experimental setup Models. We evaluated 30 models from 10 families. The closed models are seven Claude models (Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.1, Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5), three OpenAI models served through the Codex command-line interface at high reasoning effort (GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-6-Astra and GPT-6.1-Sol), Gemini 3.8 Flash, and three Gemini 4 models (Hydrogen, Argon and Carbon) through the Antigravity commandline interface at high effort (Gemini 3.8 Flash too on 4 DominoBench-124, and through the Gemini API on DominoBench-38). The open-weight models are Qwen2.5VL-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-8BThinking, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3BInstruct, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B, KimiVL-A3B-Thinking, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B, Muse Glimmer 30B, Gemma 4 31B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni, InternVL3.5-38B and dots-3-note. We call open-weight models of at most 16B parameters small and the others larger. Locally served open-weight models ran under vLLM [21] on A100, A40, L40S and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with temperature 0.6, topp 0.95, and an answer budget of 8,192 tokens, raised to 32,768 for thinking models, Gemma 4, Qwen3-VL-30BA3B and Qwen3-VL-32B, which often ran out of tokens at 8,192, and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on DominoBench-38. InternVL3.5-38B ran with FP8 weights. The other models ran with their providers default sampling. Protocol. Each combination of item, input mode and hint rung is one independent call in fresh context. The prompt holds the rules of the world, the question, the hints up to the requested rung, and either the image or the structured scene description, and it excludes the answer, the twin and the scene program. Hints identify the deciding step and may state the varied quantity. Models are asked to reason step by step, to list their assumptions, and to end with JSON object giving every persons fate and probability of death. Command-line clients ran with tools disabled or in readonly sandbox, from an empty directory holding only neutrally named copy of the image and with no user configuration or memory, so no model could read the dataset files. Antigravitys web search cannot be disabled; its prompts forbid it, and the audited transcripts show none in the reported answers. An answer that cannot be parsed, or that runs out of tokens before giving one, is scored as wrong. Evaluation sets. We report main results on two benchmark sizes, based on computational restrictions at the time of submission: calls per item (up to eight), GPU time, rate limits and available GPUs. DominoBench-1K, the full benchmark of 854 items, was answered in image mode at H0 and H3 by four Claude models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.1) and 9 open-weight models. DominoBench-124, the medium benchmark, holds the 62 remaining pairs of subset of 70 (10 per mechanism) chosen as the pairs with the most completed calls, without regard to correctness. It adds Claude Fable 5.2, Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5, the three Gemini 4 models, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6-Astra, GPT-6.1-Sol and the slower mid-sized open-weight models. For the four Claude models, exact accuracy on it is within 5 points of DominoBench-1K  (Table 1)  . We also release DominoBench-38, small, quick-torun test set of 19 separately generated pairs over six mechanisms, with the same checks; its results, including GPT-5.6Sol, which ran only there, and the full ladder for six Claude models, are in the supplement. Metrics. We report three accuracies. Exact accuracy counts an item as correct only if every fate is right. Deciding-person accuracy is computed over the person whose fate flips between the twins. Across complete pairs, valid prediction that is identical for both twins scores exactly 50% on this person, including always dies or always survives. Both-twins accuracy is the fraction of pairs in which both items are exactly right, and any answer that is the same for both twins scores zero on it (intervals: 95% Wilson, over items). DominoScore. To summarize model in one number, we combine its deciding-person accuracy over the seven mechanisms, weighting each mechanism by its difficulty. We use deciding-person accuracy alone because it is the only one of the three whose chance level is the same for every mechanism: the floor of exact accuracy depends on how many people scene holds and how often they survive, and bothtwins accuracy adds little beyond the deciding person while halving the sample to pairs. For mechanism m, let am be the deciding-person accuracy and sm = max(0, 2am 1) the skill above the 50% scored by any answer that is the same for both twins. DominoBenchs score is the weighted geometric mean DominoScore = 100 (cid:16) (cid:89) (ϵ+sm)wm ϵ (cid:17) , ϵ = 0.05, (1) which is 0 for model whose accuracy is at or below 50% on every mechanism and 100 for model that is always right. The geometric mean penalizes model that fails one mechanism outright more than an average would, and ϵ keeps single failed mechanism from setting the score to zero. The weights wm are proportional to each mechanisms difficulty, measured as the error rate on the deciding person, at H3, of the four Claude models that answered every item, with normalized weights floored at half the uniform weight and then renormalized. They are frozen and released with the benchmark, so later models are scored on the same scale: pendulum 0.300, jump 0.250, dominoes 0.152, ledge 0.092, pit 0.073, and recess and seesaw 0.066 each. We report DominoScore with 95% bootstrap interval that resamples whole twin pairs within each mechanism. Results Unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. The four Claude models that answered all 854 items predict the 6 full outcome  (Table 1)  in 3947% of items, well above the 14% of the naive chain reaction and the 25% of everyone survives. That margin comes from the people whose fate does not flip between the twins, whom these models judge correctly 8590% of the time. On the person whose fate flips, the same models are right in 5761% of items, with intervals that exclude the 50% of coin flip by only few points, and they get both twins of pair right in 1516% of pairs. In 5069% of pairs these models give the identical answer to both twins: they describe plausible chain reaction and do not register that one quantity has moved across threshold. With the calculation, the share of identical answers falls to 2224%. Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 (48% and 52%, DominoBench-124) and the open-weight models on DominoBench-1K (2553%) sit near or below chance on the deciding person and rarely get both twins right. across model The pattern holds families. On DominoBench-124, Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen are right about the deciding person in 71%, 69% and 62% of items unaided and Gemini 3.8 Flash in 52%, against 4869% for the seven Claude models, of which Claude Fable 5.2 is the most accurate unaided; with the calculation they reach 8792%, against 7591%  (Table 1)  . GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra are the most accurate unaided, on the deciding person (72% and 70%) and on the full outcome (60% and 59%), but gain least from H3 (82% and 83%), so their DominoScore at H3 (3536) trails every Gemini model and all Claude models but Haiku 4.5. The calculation helps where pointer does not. On DominoBench-124 the three Claude 5.5 models answered every rung in both modes  (Fig. 3)  . H1 adds at most 6 points, as H0 already asks models to check quantities that could change the outcome. The pointer of H2 helps Claude Sonnet 5.5 in image mode (58% to 73%) but changes little for Opus 5.5 (59% to 65%) and Haiku 5.5 (57% to 59%), while H3 lifts all three, in both modes, from 5764% to 7991%. On DominoBench-1K the effect is the same at scale: the four Claude models that answered all items rise from 57 61% to 8286% on the deciding person and from 1516% to 3449% on both twins. Knowing where to look is therefore not enough. What the strongest models lack is the step from the location of the decision to number that settles it. Coordinates given as text barely improve unaided accuracy. On DominoBench-124, the three Claude 5.5 models are right about the deciding person in 6064% of items from text and 5759% from images at H0, and in 7986% and 8291% at H3. The two modes differ by at most 6 points at H0, so misreading the picture explains little of the errors. Figure 3. Small open-weight models gain little even from the calculation. On DominoBench-1K, the small openweight models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking) and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B gain little or nothing from H3, while Muse Glimmer 30B, Gemma 4 26B-A4B, Qwen3.8-27B, dots-3-note and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL rise from 5053% to 7679% on the deciding person (DominoScore 2636). The newest larger ones reach the Claude range on DominoBench-124: Qwen3.8-27B and Muse Glimmer 30B rise from 47% and 55% to 82% and 80% on the deciding person, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 on the same items (82%). Qwen3-VL8B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B fall below chance by looping past the token budget (43% and 69% unfinished at H3). The other open-weight models on DominoBench-124. The open-weight models that ran only on DominoBench124 stay below the larger ones even with the calculation: Nemotron 3 Nano Omni, Gemma 4 31B, InternVL3.538B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B reach 6669% on the deciding person at H3 (DominoScore 1419), and Qwen3-VL8B-Thinking 56%, with 23% of its H3 answers unfinished. The six open-weight models with complete ladder  (Fig. 3)  gain nothing from H1 or H2: Mistral-Small-3.2-24B, KimiVL-A3B-Thinking, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-32B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B stay level or fall, and Qwen3-VL-8BInstruct falls from 53% at H0 to 30% at H2. With H3 only Mistral-Small-3.2-24B and Qwen3-VL-32B rise clearly (to 65% and 73%), and from text none of the six exceeds 56%. 7 Confidence. Unaided, the models are confident without being right  (Fig. 5)  : the four Claude models that answered all items give the deciding person death probability of at least 0.8 or at most 0.2 in 6376% of items, and these confident statements are correct in only 5963% (51% for the larger open-weight models, pooled). With the calculation, their confident statements are correct in 8390%. DominoScore. DominoScore (Eq. (1)) folds these permechanism results into one number per model  (Table 1)  , and we rank every model with complete run on the same 124 items of DominoBench-124  (Fig. 2)  . There, the three Gemini 4 models score highest unaided (3142, against 4 21 for the Claude models), but with the calculation they reach 6066, level with Claude Opus 5.5 (64) and within each others intervals. Unaided, the four Claude models that answered all 854 items score 1218 out of 100, and the small open-weight models score at most 2. With the calculation, the Claude models reach 4754 (Opus 5.5 highest, 54 [48, 60]) and the small open-weight models at most 11. Robustness of DominoScore. Coin-flip guessers stay below the Table 1 thresholds (95th percentiles 6.2 and 14.4 on DominoBench-1K and DominoBench-124), equal weights barely change the H3 rankings (Spearman ρ = 0.95 and 0.96), and repeat Opus 5.5 run stays inside its H3 interval (appendix). 6. Limitations DominoBench scenes are two-dimensional and drawn in single line-art style, so the benchmark does not test perception of photographs or depth. The rule that person dies when touched by any moving solid is convention that keeps outcomes categorical; it is stated with every item. Its collision boxes reach slightly beyond the drawn figures; we removed the pairs in which this decides death (Section 3). H3 supplies quantities that still image cannot show, such as speeds and thresholds calibrated in simulation, so the top rung measures the execution of stated calculation. Unaided, model must estimate those quantities from the rules and the picture, and we did not measure how well they do so. Coverage is uneven across models (Section 4), and the text-only comparison for Claude rests on DominoBench-124. We did not measure human accuracy on DominoBench. In video prediction, people surpass vision models on rolling, collision and domino scenes [5, 23]. 7. Conclusion Unaided, models do not predict these chain reactions from still image: on DominoBench-1K, the four Claude models that answered all items are only modestly better than Figure 4. Accuracy on the deciding person by deciding mechanism, from H0 (open) to H3 (filled), image mode, all 854 items. Left: Claude, right: open-weight models above DominoScore 20 at H3. Data: DominoBench-1K. Figure 5. Stated probability of death for the deciding person against how often that person dies, in bins of 0.2 (bins with at least 15 statements), image mode, all 854 items. Solid: the Claude the five larger openmodels that answered every item; dashed: weight models of Fig. 4, pooled. Dotted: perfect calibration. Data: DominoBench-1K. Mechanisms. Unaided, the Claude models are near chance  (Fig. 4)  on the recess, the dominoes and the pendulum (4957%), where the outcome depends on rotation phase, gap measured against height or the reach of swing, and they do best on the ledge, the pit and the jump (6282%). With the calculation, the recess, the seesaw and the pit rise to 84100%, the dominoes to 7795%, while the pendulum gains least among the mechanisms that start near chance (5157% to 6168%) and the jump does not move (6876% to 7172%). On both, the written-out calculation branches (a strike then swing; flight that clears or meets wall), and the Claude models often fail it. With the calculation, the five larger open-weight models of Fig. 4 rise well above chance on the dominoes, the recess and the seesaw, while the small models mostly do not. 8 coin flip on the person whose fate flips, and they usually answer both twins of pair alike. We locate the failure in the quantitative step: on DominoBench-124 neither pointer to the deciding step nor exact coordinates help the Claude models much, while on DominoBench-1K the written-out calculation brings the four Claude models to 8286% on that person. Closing this gap requires models that decide on their own which quantity scene turns on and then compute it. DominoBench tests for that ability, and its generator can produce fresh scenes as models improve.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: We used three LLM-based assistants in this project, under the authors direction and review: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), through the Claude Code CLI agent, GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI), through the Codex CLI agent, and Claude Fable 5.2 (Anthropic), for review of the draft. Ideation. The idea for the benchmark is the authors. It came from posing chain-reaction puzzle to Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6-Astra and observing that both models missed the quantities that decided the outcome until they were pointed out. We then used Claude Opus 5.5 as discussion partner while refining the design (minimal pairs, the hint ladder, the text-only mode). Code and experiments. Claude Opus 5.5 wrote most of the code for the scene generator, the physics-simulation and labelling pipeline, the evaluation harness, the analysis scripts and the figure scripts, and it launched and monitored the evaluation runs. The authors specified the design, reviewed the code and checked results against the simulator. Model-performance statistics are computed from stored responses. Dataset statistics and physical quantities come from the generated scenes and simulations. Related work. Claude Opus 5.5, through the Claude Code CLI agent, searched the literature and proposed references. Every reference was checked against Crossref or the arXiv record before inclusion. Text. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6-Astra drafted and reviewed the text of the paper from the authors instructions. The authors reviewed, revised, edited, and approved it. Models as subjects. Claude and GPT models are also among the models evaluated. They were queried in isolated sessions, the Claude models with tools disabled and the GPT models in read-only sandbox, each from temporary directory holding at most copy of the items image, with no access to the projects files, notes or prior conversation, and answered the same prompts as every other model.
